title: Safety-Critical Model Predictive Control with Discrete-Time Control Barrier Function

elements.name: MPC-CBF
elements.description: The proposed safety-critical model predictive control algorithm. At each time step t, solves a finite-horizon optimal control problem (Eq. 10) with discrete-time CBF constraints enforcing forward invariance of the safe set at every horizon step, then applies the first control input (Eq. 11) in a receding horizon fashion.
elements.source_text: The proposed control logic MPC-CBF solves the following constrained finite-time optimal control problem with horizon N at each time step t
elements.pseudocode:
At each time step t:
  1. Measure current state x_t
  2. Solve: min_{u_{t:t+N-1|t}} p(x_{t+N|t}) + sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t})
     s.t. x_{t+k+1|t} = f(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}), k=0,...,N-1
          x_{t+k|t} in X, u_{t+k|t} in U, k=0,...,N-1
          x_{t|t} = x_t
          x_{t+N|t} in X_f
          Delta_h(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}) >= -gamma * h(x_{t+k|t}), k=0,...,N-1
  3. Apply u(t) = u*_{t|t}(x_t) (first element of optimal sequence)
  4. Advance to t+1 and repeat

elements.name: System dynamics
elements.description: The discrete-time system model describing state evolution under control input.
elements.source_text: $$\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t),\tag{1}$$

elements.name: Safe set definition
elements.description: Defines the safe set C as the superlevel set of the barrier function h(x). The boundary of C is where h(x)=0.
elements.source_text: $$C = \{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^n : h(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \}. \tag{4}$$
elements.pseudocode: C = { x in X : h(x) > 0 }

elements.name: Discrete-time CBF constraint
elements.description: The core discrete-time control barrier function condition: Delta_h(x_k, u_k) > -gamma * h(x_k) with 0 < gamma < 1. This ensures h(x_{k+1}) >= (1-gamma)*h(x_k), guaranteeing exponential decay of the lower bound of h at rate (1-gamma), thus forward invariance of the safe set.
elements.source_text: $$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) > -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}_k), \ 0 < \gamma < 1,$$\nwhere  $\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) := h(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - h(\mathbf{x}_k)$ . Satisfying constraint (6), we have  $h(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) \geq (1 - \gamma)h(\mathbf{x}_k)$ , i.e., the lower bound of control barrier function h(x) decreases exponentially with the rate  $1 - \gamma$ .
elements.pseudocode: h(x_{k+1}) - h(x_k) >= -gamma * h(x_k), where 0 < gamma < 1

elements.name: CBF delta definition in MPC horizon
elements.description: Defines Delta_h in terms of predicted states along the MPC open-loop horizon: Delta_h(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}) = h(x_{t+k+1|t}) - h(x_{t+k|t}).
elements.source_text: $$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t}) = h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k+1|t}) - h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}).$$
elements.pseudocode: Delta_h(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}) = h(x_{t+k+1|t}) - h(x_{t+k|t})

elements.name: MPC-CBF optimization problem
elements.description: The main MPC-CBF formulation (Eq. 10): finite-horizon optimal control with CBF constraints at every horizon step. Replaces MPC-DC's distance constraints (Eq. 2f) with discrete-time CBF constraints (10f). This is the central contribution of the paper.
elements.source_text:
$$J_t^*(\mathbf{x}_t) = \min_{\mathbf{u}_{t:t+N-1|t}} p(\mathbf{x}_{t+N|t}) + \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t})$$
(10a)

s.t. 
$$\mathbf{x}_{t+k+1|t} = f(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t}), k = 0, ..., N-1$$
 (10b)

$$\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t} \in \mathcal{X}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t} \in \mathcal{U}, k = 0, ..., N-1$$
 (10c)

$$\mathbf{x}_{t|t} = \mathbf{x}_t, 	ag{10d}$$

$$\mathbf{x}_{t+N|t} \in \mathcal{X}_f, 	ag{10e}$$

$$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t}) \ge -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}), k = 0, ..., N-1$$
 (10f)
elements.pseudocode:
min_{u_{t:t+N-1|t}} p(x_{t+N|t}) + sum_{k=0}^{N-1} q(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t})
s.t. x_{t+k+1|t} = f(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}), k=0,...,N-1
     x_{t+k|t} in X, u_{t+k|t} in U, k=0,...,N-1
     x_{t|t} = x_t
     x_{t+N|t} in X_f
     Delta_h(x_{t+k|t}, u_{t+k|t}) >= -gamma * h(x_{t+k|t}), k=0,...,N-1

elements.name: Receding horizon feedback law
elements.description: Applies only the first element of the optimized input sequence at each time step, yielding the receding horizon control strategy.
elements.source_text: $$\mathbf{u}(t) = \mathbf{u}_{t|t}^*(\mathbf{x}_t). \tag{11}$$

elements.name: Reachable set R_k
elements.description: Defines the reachable set at horizon step k as the set of states reachable from x_t following dynamics and constraints through k steps. Used in the feasibility analysis.
elements.source_text: $$\mathcal{R}_{k} = \{\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t} \in \mathcal{X} : \forall i = 0, ..., k - 1, \\ \mathbf{x}_{t+i+1|t} = f(\mathbf{x}_{t+i|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+i|t}), \\ \mathbf{x}_{t+i|t} \in \mathcal{X}, \mathbf{u}_{t+i|t} \in \mathcal{U}, \mathbf{x}_{t|t} = \mathbf{x}_{t}\}.$$
elements.pseudocode: R_k = { x_{t+k|t} in X : for all i=0,...,k-1, x_{t+i+1|t} = f(x_{t+i|t}, u_{t+i|t}), x_{t+i|t} in X, u_{t+i|t} in U, x_{t|t} = x_t }

elements.name: CBF-enforced safe set S_cbf,k
elements.description: Defines the set of states satisfying the CBF constraint at horizon step k. The feasible region for MPC-CBF at step k is the intersection R_k intersect S_cbf,k. The level set partial S_cbf,k is where h(x) = (1-gamma)*h(x_{t+k-1|t}).
elements.source_text: $$S_{\text{cbf},k} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} : h(\mathbf{x}) - h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k-1|t}) \ge -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k-1|t}) \right\},$$
elements.pseudocode: S_cbf,k = { x in X : h(x) - h(x_{t+k-1|t}) >= -gamma * h(x_{t+k-1|t}) }

elements.name: CBF level set boundary
elements.description: The boundary of the CBF-enforced safe set at horizon step k. Smaller gamma produces tighter (smaller) safe sets, making the controller more conservative.
elements.source_text: $$\partial \mathcal{S}_{\text{cbf},k} = \{ x \in \mathcal{X} : h(\mathbf{x}) = (1 - \gamma)h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k-1|t}) \},$$
elements.pseudocode: partial S_cbf,k = { x in X : h(x) = (1 - gamma) * h(x_{t+k-1|t}) }

elements.name: MPC-CBF N=1 reduction (DCLF-DCBF comparison)
elements.description: When N=1, MPC-CBF reduces to an optimization over a single control step. The CLF constraint from DCLF-DCBF is absent (replaced by terminal cost in the objective), so no slack variable delta is needed. This shows MPC-CBF with N=1 behaves similarly to DCLF-DCBF.
elements.source_text:
$$\mathbf{u}_{k}^{*} = \underset{\mathbf{u}_{k} \in \mathbb{P}^{m}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \quad p(f(\mathbf{x}_{k}, \mathbf{u}_{k})) + q(\mathbf{x}_{k}, \mathbf{u}_{k})$$
 (14a)

$$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}_k) \ge 0, 	ag{14b}$$

$$\mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{U},$$
 (14c)
elements.pseudocode:
u*_k = argmin_{u_k} p(f(x_k, u_k)) + q(x_k, u_k)
s.t. Delta_h(x_k, u_k) + gamma * h(x_k) >= 0
     u_k in U

elements.name: DCLF-DCBF optimization (background)
elements.description: The DCLF-DCBF background method: a one-step QP that minimizes input norm with a slack variable, subject to both discrete CLF constraints and discrete CBF constraints. Used as a baseline comparison.
elements.source_text:
$$\mathbf{u}_{k}^{*} = \underset{(\mathbf{u}_{k}, \delta) \in \mathbb{R}^{m+1}}{\operatorname{argmin}} \quad \mathbf{u}_{k}^{T} H(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{u}_{k} + l \cdot \delta^{2}$$
(9a)

$$\Delta V(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + \alpha V(\mathbf{x}_k) \le \delta,$$
 (9b)

$$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) + \gamma h(\mathbf{x}_k) \ge 0,$$
 (9c)

$$\mathbf{u}_k \in \mathcal{U},$$
 (9d)
elements.pseudocode:
u*_k = argmin_{(u_k, delta)} u_k^T H(x) u_k + l * delta^2
s.t. Delta_V(x_k, u_k) + alpha * V(x_k) <= delta
     Delta_h(x_k, u_k) + gamma * h(x_k) >= 0
     u_k in U

elements.name: Stage and terminal cost (double integrator)
elements.description: Quadratic stage cost q(x_k, u_k) = x_k' Q x_k + u_k' R u_k and terminal cost p(x_N) = x_N' P x_N for the 2D double integrator experiment. Q=10*I_4, R=I_2, P=100*I_4.
elements.source_text:
$$q(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) = \mathbf{x}_k' Q \mathbf{x}_k + \mathbf{u}_k' R \mathbf{u}_k, \ p(\mathbf{x}_N) = \mathbf{x}_N' P \mathbf{x}_N,$$
 (16)
\nwhere  $Q = 10 \cdot \mathcal{I}_4$ ,  $R = \mathcal{I}_2$  and  $P = 100 \cdot \mathcal{I}_4$ .
elements.pseudocode:
q(x_k, u_k) = x_k^T @ Q @ x_k + u_k^T @ R @ u_k
p(x_N) = x_N^T @ P @ x_N
Q = 10 * I_4, R = I_2, P = 100 * I_4

elements.name: 2D double integrator dynamics
elements.description: Linear discrete-time dynamics for the 2D double integrator: x_{k+1} = A x_k + B u_k, with sampling time dt=0.2s. State includes 2D position and velocity.
elements.source_text: $$\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = A\mathbf{x}_k + B\mathbf{u}_k,\tag{15}$$\nwhere the sampling time  $\Delta t$  is set as 0.2s.
elements.pseudocode: x_{k+1} = A @ x_k + B @ u_k, with dt = 0.2s

elements.name: State and input bounds (double integrator)
elements.description: Box constraints on state (X) and input (U) for the double integrator experiment. State bounds +/-5 in each component, input bounds +/-1.
elements.source_text:
$$\mathcal{X} = \{\mathbf{x}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n : \mathbf{x}_{\min} \le \mathbf{x}_k \le \mathbf{x}_{\max}\},\\
\mathcal{U} = \{\mathbf{u}_k \in \mathbb{R}^m : \mathbf{u}_{\min} \le \mathbf{u}_k \le \mathbf{u}_{\max}\}.$$
\nThe lower and upper bounds are

$$\mathbf{x}_{\max}, \mathbf{x}_{\min} = \pm 5 \cdot \mathcal{I}_{4 \times 1}, \ \mathbf{u}_{\max}, \mathbf{u}_{\min} = \pm \mathcal{I}_{2 \times 1}.$$
elements.pseudocode:
X = { x: x_min <= x <= x_max }, where x_max = 5, x_min = -5
U = { u: u_min <= u <= u_max }, where u_max = 1, u_min = -1

elements.name: Quadratic barrier function (obstacle avoidance)
elements.description: The barrier function for the 2D double integrator obstacle avoidance task. h_k = (x - x_obs)^2 + (y - y_obs)^2 - r_obs^2. The obstacle is at (-2, -2.25) with radius 1.5m. Safe region is where h > 0 (outside the obstacle circle).
elements.source_text:
$$h_k = (\mathbf{x}_k(1) - x_{obs})^2 + (\mathbf{x}_k(2) - y_{obs})^2 - r_{obs}^2,$$
 (17)
\nwhere  $x_{obs}$ ,  $y_{obs}$ , and  $r_{obs}$  describe x/y-coordinate and radius of the obstacle with  $x_{obs} = -2m$ ,  $y_{obs} = -2.25m$  and  $r_{obs} = 1.5m$ , shown as a red circle in Fig. 4.
elements.pseudocode:
h_k = (x_k[0] - x_obs)^2 + (x_k[1] - y_obs)^2 - r_obs^2
x_obs = -2, y_obs = -2.25, r_obs = 1.5

elements.name: Nonlinear vehicle dynamics (car racing)
elements.description: Full nonlinear lateral vehicle dynamics model in curvilinear(Frenet) coordinates for the car racing scenario. State is 6D: [vx, vy, phi, e_phi, s, e_y], input is 2D: [a, delta].
elements.source_text:
$$\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{u}_t), \tag{18}$$\nwhere  $x_t$  and  $u_t$  represent the state and input of the vehicle at time step t and their definitions are as follow

$$\mathbf{x}_t = [v_{x_t}, \ v_{y_t}, \ \phi_t, \ e_{\phi_t}, \ s_t, \ e_{y_t}]^T, \ \mathbf{u}_t = [a_t, \ \delta_t]^T,$$
 (19)
elements.pseudocode:
x = [vx, vy, phi, e_phi, s, e_y], u = [a, delta]
x_{t+1} = f(x_t, u_t) (nonlinear lateral vehicle dynamics)

elements.name: Vehicle state and input definitions
elements.description: Defines the 6D state vector (longitudinal velocity, lateral velocity, yaw rate, heading error, curvilinear distance, lateral deviation) and 2D input vector (acceleration, steering angle) in curvilinear coordinates.
elements.source_text:
$$\mathbf{x}_t = [v_{x_t}, \ v_{y_t}, \ \phi_t, \ e_{\phi_t}, \ s_t, \ e_{y_t}]^T, \ \mathbf{u}_t = [a_t, \ \delta_t]^T,$$
 (19)
elements.pseudocode:
x_t = [vx_t, vy_t, phi_t, e_phi_t, s_t, e_y_t]
u_t = [a_t, delta_t]

elements.name: Racing stage cost (tracking centerline at target speed)
elements.description: Stage cost for the car racing MPC: tracks centerline with target speed while minimizing control effort. xr = (vt, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), Q=diag(10,0,0,0,0,0,10), R=diag(1,1). The Q matrix penalizes deviation from target longitudinal speed.
elements.source_text:
$$q(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t}, \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t}) = (\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t} - \mathbf{x}_r)^T Q(\mathbf{x}_{t+k|t} - \mathbf{x}_r) + \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t}^T R \mathbf{u}_{t+k|t},$$(20)

where  $\mathbf{x}_r = (v_t, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)$ , Q = diag(10, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 10) and R = diag(1, 1). This cost function allows the ego car to track the centerline with a target speed  $v_t$  while minimizing the tracking error from the centerline.

elements.name: Quartic barrier function (car racing)
elements.description: Quartic CBF for car-car collision avoidance in curvilinear coordinates. Models each car as a rectangle of size 2l1 x 2l2. The barrier function ensures the ego car maintains safe distance from the i-th racing car.
elements.source_text:
$$h_t^i = \frac{(s_t - s_t^i)^4}{(2l_1)^4} + \frac{(e_{y_t} - e_{y_t}^i)^4}{(2l_2)^4} - 1,$$
 (21)

where we assume all racing cars including ego car hold the shape of rectangle with a length as  $2l_1$  and width as  $2l_2$ .

elements.name: Linearized vehicle dynamics for optimization
elements.description: The nonlinear vehicle dynamics is linearized around the centerline trajectory (obtained via a PID pre-simulation) using a regression-based data-driven approach. The resulting linear time-invariant model x_{t+1} = A x_t + B u_t is used in the MPC optimization to reduce computational burden.
elements.source_text: $$\mathbf{x}_{t+1} = A\mathbf{x}_t + B\mathbf{u}_t,\tag{22}$$\nwhere A and B are calculated with a regression-based approach [27] over the trajectory we simulated using a PID controller.
elements.pseudocode: x_{t+1} = A @ x_t + B @ u_t (linearized, data-driven)

elements.name: PID controller for trajectory linearization
elements.description: PID controller used to generate centerline trajectory data for the regression-based linearization. delta = -k1*e_y - k2*e_psi for steering, a = k3*(vd - vx) for longitudinal acceleration.
elements.source_text:
$$\delta_t = -k_1 e_{y_t} - k_2 e_{\psi_t}, a_t = k_3 (v_d - v_{x_t}),$$
where  $v_d$  could be any positive user-defined target speed.
elements.pseudocode:
delta_t = -k1 * e_y_t - k2 * e_psi_t
a_t = k3 * (vd - vx_t)

elements.name: MPC-CBF unified framework
elements.description: The core concept of unifying model predictive control with discrete-time control barrier functions into a single optimization problem. CBF constraints enforce safe set invariance at every horizon step, enabling proactive obstacle avoidance even when the robot is far from obstacles, unlike MPC-DC which only activates constraints when the reachable set intersects unsafe regions.
elements.source_text: we present a safety-critical model predictive control strategy utilizing discrete-time control barrier functions (CBFs), which guarantees system safety and accomplishes optimal performance via model predictive control.

elements.name: Safe set invariance via CBF
elements.description: The concept that satisfying the CBF constraint ensures forward invariance of the safe set C: if h(x_0) >= 0 and 0 < gamma <= 1, then the safe set remains invariant along trajectories. This provides formal safety guarantees beyond heuristics.
elements.source_text: The safe set  $\mathcal{C}$  in (4) is invariant along the trajectories of the discrete-time system with controller (9) if  $h(\mathbf{x}_0) \geq 0$  and  $0 < \gamma \leq 1$ .

elements.name: Feasibility via reachable-set / safe-set intersection
elements.description: The feasibility of MPC-CBF at each horizon step k is determined by whether the intersection R_k intersect S_cbf,k is nonempty. Gamma controls the tradeoff: smaller gamma makes S_cbf,k smaller (safer but potentially infeasible), larger gamma makes it larger (more feasible but less constraining).
elements.source_text: the feasibility of the optimization in (10) turns out to be whether the intersection between the feasible set at each horizon step,  $\mathcal{R}_k$ , and the superlevel set of  $h(\mathbf{x})$  satisfying the CBF constraints,  $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cbf},k}$ , is nonempty for all k=1,...,N.

elements.name: Receding horizon strategy
elements.description: The MPC-CBF optimization is solved at each time step with the latest measured state. Only the first input of the optimized sequence is applied, and the problem is re-solved at the next step with updated state measurements.
elements.source_text: This constrained finite-time optimal control problem (10) is repeated at time step t+1, based on the new state  $\mathbf{x}_{t+1|t+1}$ , yielding a receding horizon control strategy: safety-critical model predictive control (MPC-CBF).

elements.name: Gamma tradeoff (safety vs feasibility)
elements.description: The gamma parameter controls a fundamental tradeoff between safety and optimization feasibility. Small gamma: the safe set shrinks, making the controller more conservative and safe, but potentially causing infeasibility. Large gamma: the safe set expands, improving feasibility but making CBF constraints potentially inactive (not confining the reachable set).
elements.source_text: Remark 3: When  $\gamma$  becomes relatively small, the MPC-CBF controller makes a smaller subset of the safe set  $\mathcal C$  in (4) invariant, and thus is more safer, but this might also make the optimization infeasible. A larger  $\gamma$  will make the optimization more likely to be feasible, but the CBF constraints might not be active during the optimization.

elements.name: NLP nature of MPC-CBF optimization
elements.description: The MPC-CBF optimization is generally a nonlinear programming (NLP) problem because the discrete-time CBF constraints are non-convex unless the barrier functions are linear. Solvers like IPOPT are used.
elements.source_text: The discrete-time control barrier functions constraints in (10f) are generally non-convex unless the CBFs are linear. This makes the whole optimization in (10) generally become a nonlinear programming problem (NLP).

elements.name: Curvilinear coordinate system
elements.description: The car racing experiment uses curvilinear (Frenet) coordinates to describe vehicle states relative to the track centerline. This includes longitudinal distance s, lateral deviation e_y, heading error e_phi, and velocities in the Frenet frame.
elements.source_text: We use curvilinear coordinates to describe vehicle states of the ego and other cars in a racing competition.

elements.name: 2D double integrator obstacle avoidance
elements.description: Primary validation experiment: a 2D double integrator starting at (-5,-5) navigates to (0,0) while avoiding a circular obstacle at (-2,-2.25) with radius 1.5m. Compares MPC-CBF against DCLF-DCBF (N=1 baseline) and MPC-DC (distance-constraint baseline). Benchmarks different horizons N and gamma values in Table I for computational time, min distance, and cost integral.
elements.source_text: Consider a linear discrete-time 2D double integrator... A MPC-CBF is designed as in (10) and (11) for 2D double integrator to avoid an obstacle... The start and target positions are (-5, -5) and (0, 0).

elements.name: Competitive car racing
elements.description: Complex validation experiment: an ego car races on a track with two other racing cars, safely overtaking them. Uses quartic CBF for car-car collision avoidance, linearized vehicle dynamics for optimization, N=12 horizon at 10Hz, target speed 0.6 m/s. Two opponent cars at 0.2 m/s with lateral offsets +0.1m and -0.1m.
elements.source_text: MPC-CBF with a horizon N = 12 updates at 10 Hz... Our ego vehicle is simulated with the nonlinear lateral vehicle dynamics model and we use the linearized dynamics along the centerline to formulate our control design... two other racing cars start in front of the ego car. Two cars are simulated to move at 0.2 m/s while keeping a constant distance deviation  $e_y^i$  from the centerline, where  $e_y^1=0.1~{\rm m}$  and  $e_y^2=-0.1~{\rm m}$ .

elements.name: Stability guarantee via terminal cost as CLF
elements.description: The terminal cost p(x_{t+N|t}) in MPC-CBF serves as a control Lyapunov function, which can guarantee closed-loop stability under mild assumptions for linear systems. This bridges the gap with DCLF-DCBF which uses explicit CLF constraints.
elements.source_text: In our MPC-CBF control design, we have the terminal cost  $p(\mathbf{x}_{t+N|t})$  in (10a) as a control Lyapunov function, which can be used to guarantee the stability of the closed-loop system by satisfying mild assumptions in the context of linear systems [18, Thm. 12.2].

elements.name: MPC-CBF N=1 is equivalent to DCLF-DCBF
elements.description: When prediction horizon N=1, MPC-CBF reduces to a formulation similar to DCLF-DCBF: the CLF constraint from DCLF-DCBF becomes the terminal cost in the objective, and the slack variable is removed. This validates the consistency of MPC-CBF with the one-step DCLF-DCBF method.
elements.source_text: Remark 5: As the CLF constraints in (9b) are transferred into the cost function in (14) with N=1, the formulation in (14) becomes similar to DCLF-DCBF. To sum up, our MPC-CBF formulation operates in a similar manner of DCLF-DCBF with prediction N=1.

elements.name: MPC-CBF with gamma=1 approximates MPC-DC
elements.description: When gamma approaches 1, the CBF constraint becomes h(x_{t+k+1|t}) >= 0, which is almost the same as MPC-DC's distance constraint g(x_{t+k|t}) >= 0 (one step difference). The feasible sets become comparable.
elements.source_text:
When  $\gamma$  approaches its upper bound of 1, the CBF constraints in (10f) becomes,

h(\mathbf{x}_{t+k+1|t}) \ge 0.

If  $g(\mathbf{x})$  in (2f) and  $h(\mathbf{x})$  are the same, these CBF constraints are almost the same as distance constraints defined in (2f)

elements.name: MPC-CBF is safer than MPC-DC (smaller set invariance)
elements.description: MPC-CBF's feasible set R_k intersect S_cbf,k is a proper subset of MPC-DC's feasible set R_k intersect C (since S_cbf,k is a subset of C). This makes MPC-CBF more conservative and safer, even when far from obstacles.
elements.source_text: Remark 7: Our MPC-CBF formulation is safer than MPC-DC in the context of smaller set invariance, where we can see that  $\mathcal{R}_k \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{cbf},k}$  is a proper subset of  $\mathcal{R}_k \cap \mathcal{C}$ , as shown in Fig. 3.

elements.name: Smaller gamma enables smaller horizon (Remark 8)
elements.description: MPC-CBF with a smaller gamma and smaller prediction horizon N can achieve comparable obstacle avoidance performance to MPC-DC with a much larger horizon. This reduces computational complexity since the CBF constraints proactively confine the reachable set even at short horizons.
elements.source_text: Remark 8: In practice, we may need to use a smaller horizon for speeding up the optimization. To achieve a similar performance compared to the MPC-DC formulation in (2), we could apply smaller  $\gamma$  in our MPC-CBF control design in (10) and use a smaller horizon.

elements.name: Prediction horizon N
elements.description: MPC prediction horizon length. Used as N=1 (DCLF-DCBF equivalent), N=5, N=8 in double integrator experiments, and N=12 in car racing. Controls the tradeoff between performance and computational cost.
elements.source_text: The proposed control logic MPC-CBF solves the following constrained finite-time optimal control problem with horizon N at each time step t

elements.name: CBF decay rate gamma
elements.section: Section II-B, Section III-C, Section IV
elements.description: The CBF decay rate parameter controlling safe set shrinkage per step. Range 0 < gamma < 1. Used values: gamma=0.4 (vs DCLF-DCBF), gamma=0.1,0.2,0.25,0.3,0.5 (horizon comparisons), gamma=1.0 (MPC-DC comparison). Smaller gamma yields more conservative (safer) behavior.
elements.source_text: $$\Delta h(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) > -\gamma h(\mathbf{x}_k), \ 0 < \gamma < 1,$$

elements.name: Cost matrices Q, R, P
elements.description: Positive definite weighting matrices for stage cost (Q, R) and terminal cost (P). Double integrator: Q=10*I_4, R=I_2, P=100*I_4. Racing: Q=diag(10,0,0,0,0,0,10), R=diag(1,1).
elements.source_text: where  $Q = 10 \cdot \mathcal{I}_4$ ,  $R = \mathcal{I}_2$  and  $P = 100 \cdot \mathcal{I}_4$ .

elements.name: Controller sampling time
elements.description: Controller update interval: dt=0.2s for double integrator, dt=0.1s (10Hz) for car racing. The system dynamics simulation runs at 1000Hz for racing.
elements.source_text: where the sampling time  $\Delta t$  is set as 0.2s.

elements.name: Obstacle and initial/target configuration
elements.description: Double integrator scenario parameters: obstacle at (-2, -2.25) with radius 1.5m, start position (-5,-5), target position (0,0).
elements.source_text: with  $x_{obs} = -2m$ ,  $y_{obs} = -2.25m$  and  $r_{obs} = 1.5m$ , shown as a red circle in Fig. 4. The start and target positions are (-5, -5) and (0, 0),

elements.name: Racing scenario parameters
elements.description: Car racing parameters: target speed vt=0.6 m/s, initial speed v0=0.2 m/s, two opponent cars at 0.2 m/s with lateral offsets +0.1m and -0.1m, car rectangle dimensions 2l1 x 2l2, N=12 horizon at 10Hz.
elements.source_text: MPC-CBF with a horizon N = 12 updates at 10 Hz... Ego car begins with an initial speed  $v_0 = 0.2$  m/s at the origin of the centerline and two other racing cars start in front of the ego car. Two cars are simulated to move at 0.2 m/s while keeping a constant distance deviation  $e_y^i$  from the centerline, where  $e_y^1=0.1~{\rm m}$  and  $e_y^2=-0.1~{\rm m}$ .

elements.name: CLF decay rate alpha (DCLF-DCBF)
elements.description: The decay rate for the discrete-time CLF in DCLF-DCBF. Used in the CLF constraint Delta_V + alpha*V <= 0 with 0 < alpha <= 1. Only relevant for DCLF-DCBF baseline, not MPC-CBF.
elements.source_text: $$\Delta V(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k) \le -\alpha V(\mathbf{x}_k), \ 0 < \alpha \le 1,$$
